It is my pleasure to submit the annual report on the activities of the Office of the Town Manager during
Fiscal Year 2022. Fiscal Year 2022 started off like most other years however, there were lingering after
effects of the pandemic. The pandemic brought about a shift in the employment marketplace, causing
vacancies to last longer and a smaller applicant pool to fill positions. The State extended the allowance of
virtual public meetings, which most boards and committees continued to use as a matter of convenience and,
at times, for personal health reasons. The federal stimulus funds that were part of the American Rescue Plan
Act made their way down to cities and towns and this would result in many discussions in how best to use
these windfall monies. Driver shortages, supply chain issues, and increased demand for items disrupted our
Pay As You Throw program, severely impacted the delivery schedule of vehicles/equipment the Department
of Public Works, Fire Department, and Police Department ordered and spiked costs for construction projects.
Despite the ripple effects of the pandemic, the Town continued to provide a high level of services and was
another year of progress. Below I would like to highlight the topics that were addressed and the
accomplishments within the Office of the Town Manager:
• In July of 2021, as part of the annual goal setting process, the Selectmen reviewed and voted to accept the
Town Manager's annual goals for FY22. The Town Manager's goals for FY22 included continuing to
take the necessary steps towards the redevelopment/reuse of 925 Massachusetts Avenue, working with
the Select Board on creating a means tested senior citizen tax relief program, and action items related to
enhancing facilities maintenance and management. A majority of the action items related to these three
goals were completed. In regards to 925 Massachusetts Avenue, the Town Manager continued to work
Joe McLaughlin of BETA Group, MassDEP, and MassDevelopment about possible cleanup funding. In
the end we worked with the EPA and this project was put on the list of projects in line for federal funding
through Targeted Brownfields Assessment funding. The funding would pay for removal of the
underground tanks, limited soil removal and make the Town eligible for future cleanup funds. This work
is slated to be completed in FY 2023. In addition, a survey was completed for the property and after
much due diligence to eliminate any possibility that the Town would be legally responsible for cleanup,
the Town foreclosed on the property, which was a necessary step to receive the federal funding from the
EPA.As it related to one of the action items under the Town Manager's annual goals for Facilities, the
Town Manager followed the Town Charter process for an Administrative Organization Plan and after a
public hearing process, received approval at the May 2022 Annual Town Meeting to separate Facilities
from the Department of Public Works. The third goal, to assist the Select Board with a means tested
senior citizen tax relief program was initiated and the Principal Assessor presented information from
other communities with similar programs to the working group. Ultimately additional time was needed to
develop the framework of the program and its effects on taxpayers, so this goal was carried forward to
• In July 2021, the Select Board set their goals for the upcoming year: they amended their FY21 goal/work
on the old Primary School at 30 School Street with additional action items such as engaging with a
landscape architecture firm to discuss a vision of multi-use, passive recreation/ green space project at the
site and all necessary steps to bring the associated costs to the 2022 Annual Town Meeting. Another goal
was to work with the Town Manager and Finance Director to establish a means-tested senior citizen
property tax exemption or abatement. The last goal was to develop a policy designed to encourage
volunteerism in Town, specifically for town boards, committees, and commissions. A Request for
Proposals was put out twice for selection of a landscape architect for 30 School Street and ultimately
architect Ray Dunetz was chosen for the project. Various staff and community meetings led to a
conceptual design that requested additional funding at the May 2022 Annual Town Meeting, but funding
was only approved for abatement and demolition of the structure and the associated engineering costs.
The goal of developing a policy designed to encourage volunteerism was discussed at a workshop but the
Board was split on the language of the policy so no action was taken during fiscal year 2022 on this goal.
• At the end of Fiscal Year 2021 the Town received a letter from Mass Housing that Pond View
Commons, LLC had filed an application for a 40B housing project. The proposed development would
consist of 200 units of rental housing on 18.5 acres of land located at 318, 390 & 400 Howard Street.
• August 2022 began with a workshop on Chapter 40B led by Town Counsel Adam Costa on the role of the
Zoning Board of Appeals would provide in the application process. The Town was required to submit a
response to the letter from Mass Housing by September 2, 2021, which an 88-page response was
submitted that included numerous letters from residents, town boards, town counsel, and the Town
Manager. Mass Housing reviewed the town's response, requested information from the applicant and
ultimately granted a positive 40B project eligibility in March of 2022. From that point on, the applicant
filed a comprehensive permit application with the Zoning Board of Appeals. The application is still
ongoing as of writing this report.

• As previously mentioned, Fiscal Year 2022 was a difficult year for retaining staff and filling vacancies.
The pandemic created opportunities for employees to move to new careers and made it a more competitive
marketplace for employers. The Assistant Town Manager/HR Director who is responsible for advertising
vacancies and working with the relevant departments to bring on new employees was constantly reviewing
applications, interviewing and trying to fill vacancies throughout the year. In August 2021 the Veterans
Agent, IT Director (shared between Town/School), and a Board Clerk resigned. The Veterans Agent
position was filled in September, the Town Manager hired an outside consultant in September to fill the
role of the IT Director, and additional Board Clerks were hired throughout the year. In September
Principal Assessor Sue Byrne announced her retirement effective end of September and Christine Kumar
was hired in September to fill this position, but resigned at the end of November. The position was filled
with a temporary Assessor, Rena Swezey, from December 2021 until March of 2022 when Christopher
Carroll was selected to fill the permanent position. In October the Principal Clerk for the Town
Accountant retired and this position changed to an Assistant Town Accountant position after the
November Special Town Meeting and was filled in January 2022. Also in October the Recreation Director
Kayla Wright resigned and Rob Thompson was hired in December to fill this position. In March DPW
Director Rob Oliva resigned and this position was unfilled until May of 2022 when Bill Bernard was
appointed. Also in May of 2022 Conservation Administrator Matt Marro retired and Nadia Madden was
hired in May to fill this position. The Police Department also saw staffing changes with three Reserve and
Full-Time Officers leaving for other positions, and these were filled at different times during the year. The
DPW had up to three vacant Heavy Equipment Operator positions at all times during the year. The
Council on Aging and Public Access also had vacancies for Van Drivers and Videographers during the
fiscal year as well. The positions that were new to the FY22 budget, including the Assistant to the Sewer
Business Manager position, Board/Committee Clerk positions, Remote Meeting Coordinator, Trash &
Recycling Coordinator, an additional Police Officer, an additional Firefighter/Paramedic, and restoration
of a Facilities Technician position, were all filled at various times during the year.

• This year was another productive year for infrastructure projects in Lunenburg. Through a $260,000

The Board of Assessors is responsible for establishing the value of property, both real and personal, for
taxation purposes for the town. Assessed values are subject to a five-year revaluation and interim year
adjustments for certification by the Department of Revenue. The Assessors grant all statutory exemptions for
Senior and Surviving Spouse, Blind and Veterans. They act on all abatement applications to property values.
The Assessors are responsible for defending all appeals to the Appellate Tax Board. They also administer all
special assessments qualifying farm and forest management programs. Assessments in Massachusetts are
based on full and fair cash value as of January 1st.
The Assessors analyze all sales from 2021 for FY 23 valuations. Market value has seen increases in the sales
of homes in town. Properties have been selling over the assessed valuations reflecting an overall increase to
market value of the town. The next town wide recertification will occur this year for FY 2024.
Each property in town has a property record card on file with all the components that go into the valuation of
the parcel - such as land size, building description, sales information, etc. We recommend that the taxpayers
review their property field card annually to ensure all the information is up to date and correct. The property
record cards are available in our office or online through the GIS maps.
The Department of Revenue certified the results of assessment data to be within their statistical requirements
and the tax bills went out on time. The tax rate went from $17.19 to $14.62 for FY 2023.
The office continues the process of mandated cyclical inspections of all properties throughout the town. This
is achieved by inspections, visiting the properties, and by means of sales verification, building permits,
occupancy permits and abatement inspections. The Board of Assessors strives to maintain accuracy in the
assessment to sales ratio as well as assessment uniformity.
The office staff strives to continue to provide good service that the Lunenburg taxpayers have come to expect.

Armed with all the information gathered during this process, the Finance Committee recommends approval of the Town

Overall, our financial condition is good. Revenues are stable, aided by strong collections, increases in state aid, new
growth, and a variety of federal and state grants that the town has secured. On the expense side, while not meeting every
need outlined by the department heads, this budget does begin to address several emerging and previously unmet needs.
The total in requested expenditures is $49,953,531.76. While we are pleased with our current fiscal standing, we do face
challenges ahead; especially with regard to a number of our municipal buildings, which we outline in more detail below.
Notably, our certified free cash this year is $2,666,962, which is substantially higher than in previous years, a temporary
benefit resulting from appropriations that were not fully expended in FY21 as a result of COVID-related restrictions and
impacts. Town fiscal policy directs portions of free cash to accounts such as stabilization, the OPEB allocation (a fund to
pay for future retiree benefits), and the capital plan.
Accordingly, this year's recommended capital plan (funded by free cash, tax revenues, and unspent capital
appropriations from previous years) is $2,162,849. It is an unprecedented investment of available funds (without
incurring any additional debt) into the capital infrastructure that supports our town. As of the printing of this warrant, the
Finance Committee is seeking to answer a few specific questions pertaining to the capital plan. We will have a
recommendation on the capital plan, Article 6, at Town Meeting on May 7.

As the pandemic stretched into Fiscal Year 2022, we saw lingering disruption of old patterns and new patterns of
behavior continuing. One constant, however, seems to repeat itself: the library builds value for the community.
The library has continued to follow its strategic plan this year. Keeping our mission close to our hearts:
Lunenburg Public Library welcomes all and serves residents of the Lunenburg area as a hub for the community,
enriching our lives through its collections, programs, services, facility, and people.
Our library resources reach far into the community. You no longer need to visit the library in person to access our
resources. The library has focused on improving and expanding the number of resources available digitally, and made
concerted efforts to ease access to those resources. We also added Niche Academy to help patrons learn about our digital
resources and how to access them. Another new resource that will be much appreciated is Mango Languages, offering a
convenient way to learn over 70 foreign languages, with a focus on conversations.
Patrons can use all of our databases, e-books and e-audiobooks, our website (lunenburglibrary.org), and even streaming
services like Kanopy from their homes or cars or workplace. You could even attend a virtual program or interact with
library staff for help on a question or a reading recommendation without visiting the library. Of course, if you never
visited, you would be missing out on the beautiful building.
You would also be missing out on one of the most important services we offer: library programs. Although attendance in
-person during FY22 was not as consistent as it was immediately before the pandemic, there are still programs
happening at the library nearly every day, and our consistency paid dividends during the summer, as attendance at
programs really returned to a normal level. During the year library statt tocused on providing access to programs
virtually and in-person, and continuing to build a dependable, consistent calendar of events that would appeal to a variety
Library staff have also focused on trying to find new ways for residents to engage with our library collection.
Particularly worthy of note are curated experiences that have been very popular. Individuals even travel from nearby
communities to try out these kits. Our Adult Services Librarian, Lydia Gravel, introduced the idea with "Mystery Travel
Kits" which create an enriching learning experience mimicking some parts of travelling to a foreign country by using
items in the library collection. Each kit typically contains several books, a movie or two, music, and some activities or
games. These kits are still being curated and can be requested through our online event calendar on our website.
As the year went on, we saw more and more people actually visiting the library. Each afternoon during the school year,
we have been seeing more students than ever before. Partnering with the Boys and Girls Club brings dozens of students
to study during the afternoon Power Hour. In addition to that, we often see dozens of other teens, spending time at the
library. They play video games, study quietly, eat snacks, and sometimes make a little too much noise. We are, however,
excited that they have chosen to come to the library after school.
We continue to focus on stewarding the facility for the future. Efficiency and sustainability are priorities for the trustees
and the director. This year we completed replacement of a number of lighting fixtures and bulbs, so that we are now
almost completely lit by LEDs. The HVAC system has also been at the forefront of our attention, as it is beginning to
show the signs of its age. Increased maintenance needs are typical of an aging system, and ours is no exception. We will
continue to make responsible plans for the facility, so that it will be a gem for Lunenburg for decades to come.

The Sewer Commission bears the responsibility of overseeing the Sewer Enterprise Fund, planning for the future, and
developing and implementing rules, regulations and policies. Under the Town's Charter, responsibility for the day-to-
day operation, care and maintenance of the sanitary sewers are under the supervision of the Town Manager who
delegates the responsibility to manage and maintain the operational side of the system to the Department of Public
Works Director. The Town of Lunenburg does not operate a sewer treatment plant. Approximately 86% of Lunenburg
sewer is discharged to the City of Leominster, and the other 14% is discharged to the City of Fitchburg.

needs of its Veterans. Lunenburg has a part-time VSO at the Ritter Building at 960 Massachusetts Ave.

military service or veteran status. On a monthly basis, the veterans and widows of veterans in Lunenburg
receive in excess of $328,330.74 in federal benefits (Veterans Administration), which they mostly put back
into the community by paying their taxes and through discretionary spending.

specitic living expenses such as heating fuel, medical care, and pharmaceutical co-payments. With the VSO's
approval, the Town of Lunenburg provides the financial assistance and is then reimbursed by the state's
department of Veterans' Services (DVS). It is the function of the Veterans' Services Office to identify
qualifying members of the community and assist with enrollment into the DVS program. Additionally, certain
Veterans and/or widows may also be eligible for federal benefits from the Veterans Administration (VA).
Only Massachusetts offers both of these services to every community.

Regional Emergency Communications Centers in the State of Massachusetts, opening its doors on June 18, 2013.

businesses, and attractions within its six communities. In 2022, NVRDD handled 33,500 phone calls coming in on 911

services. While the focus is on handling emergencies, our staff also serves the public and our responders by providing
other administrative and non-emergency dispatch tasks. NVRDD staffs the communications center with multiple
dispatchers and supervisors each shift to handle calls and requests.

report entered into the Computer Aided Dispatch system by the dispatchers for the 9-1-1 calls

learning at all levels, and promoting the development of attributes and skills necessary for continuous learning for all.
The Strategy is a living document. Each August the District Leadership Team reviews the Strategy, its objectives and
action plans. The Strategy objectives for the next two to three years are:
Transforming Teaching and Learning: To ensure teaching and learning are student-centered and inclusive
by: (1) establishing effective teams of educational leaders to accomplish the essential work for transforming
practice, and (2) hiring and developing excellent educators who are continually learning and adapting practice to
meet the needs of all students.
Cultivating Climate & Culture: To create a culture that values data use and fosters continuous learning in
a climate that is safe, caring, inclusive and reflective of our core values.
Communication & Operations: To improve operational efficiencies, including communication, in order to
increase the organization's capacity to execute the district's mission and vision.
Equity, Access, Achievement & Opportunity for All Students: To ensure all students are provided equal
access to a high-quality education, that is collaborative, interactive, and relevant with an appropriate level of
support and challenge so that they can become well-rounded, resilient, confident, and capable young adults
Over the last several years we have worked to put in place the necessary infrastructure to support the academic
achievement of all students. We have established curriculum leadership positions, instructional specialists/coaches,
teacher curriculum leaders; piloted and purchased evidence-based math and literacy curricula for Kindergarten (K)
through grade 5; implemented a standards-based benchmark assessment in math and literacy for grades K through 8;
provided job-embedded professional development for teachers in best instructional practices and using assessment data
to inform their instruction; and hired tutoring/intervention staff for additional academic supports during the school day as
well as after school in order to close learning gaps. The Director of Teaching and Learning and Title I Coordinator
positions have been and continue to be integral to all of this work.

The district has been working with intent to foster a safe and caring environment and inclusive culture in our schools and
district. Last year we administered the National School Climate Center survey for families, students, and staff. We
analyzed results and used that data to develop goals to improve our schools' climate. We will repeat that survey this
spring to see if changes have had any impact. As we look to build a more inclusive culture in our schools, we also look
to diversify our staff to be more reflective of our community. To that end, a district team participated in the Department
of Elementary and Secondary Education's Teacher Diversification Professional Learning Network and as a result, have
been examining our recruitment and hiring practices. The Lunenburg School Committee is also committed to this work
and requested an equity audit for our district. The audit commenced in July 2022 and the final report was made available
to the Lunenburg community in February 2023 via the district website with a request for feedback. The District
Leadership will use this report to develop action plans which will be included in the district's Strategy for Continuous
Improvement. Once these plans are developed, as is our annual practice, the administration will seek the Lunenburg
School Committee's endorsement. We look forward to engaging in this work with stakeholders.
Another way the district is seeking to build a more inclusive culture is through strengthening the family-school
partnership. This year Luneburg Public Schools was one of four districts/schools selected to participate in the
Department of Elementary and Secondary Education's Family-School Partnership Initiative Program. We will be
expanding this work to involve stakeholders. This work will also result in the development of action plans, which will be
incorporated into the Strategy for Continuous Improvement.
It is important to note that the physical environment of our schools is also important to the learning experience of our
students. Turkey Hill Elementary School is an aging facility which was not designed for elementary age students. It was
originally a middle school. The building presents challenges and limitations for our teachers in terms of delivery of
instruction in the modern era. Electrical outlets are extremely limited in the classrooms and the lack of energy efficient
windows creates a challenging learning environment with very high and very low outdoor temperatures. The building
has aging systems that cannot be easily, quickly, or inexpensively addressed. With each passing year, the risk of system
failures looms larger. It is important for the school district administration, School Committee, and other boards and
committees to continue to engage in discussion regarding the future of Turkey Hill Elementary School.
All of these individual efforts and discussions regarding the future are designed to have a cumulative impact on student
achievement and growth, and overall well-being in the post-COVID years and beyond. I wish to acknowledge and thank
our staff for their professionalism and flexibility as we have continued to make adjustments in order to provide the best
possible learning environment and experience for our students; our parents and families for their continued support and
partnership; and the Lunenburg School Committee, Town Manager, and local boards and committees for their support of
the schools. We remain focused on improving the ways in which we support our students academically, socially and
emotionally in partnership with parents, extended families, and the greater community. Through this work we are on a
journey together. Collectively we have been and will continue to make a difference for our students. I think Maya
Angelou has captured our journey well when she said, "I have great respect for the past. If you don't know where
you've come from, you don't know where you're going. I have respect for the past, but I'm a person of the moment.
I'm here, and I do my best to be completely centered at the place I'm at, then I go forward to the next place."

efforts of the staff to implement PBIS over the last two years. We have also noticed fewer repeat offenders as restorative
justice is teaching students about accepting responsibility for their behavior.
Our school's success relies upon the combined and collaborative efforts of our wonderful staff, parents, and community
members. We continue to seek out opportunities to engage and effectively communicate with our families. Turkey Hill
may be a well-worn building, constructed in 1969, but it is also a well-loved and cared for community of students
supported by parents, staff, and Lunenburg residents. I am honored to serve as principal.
Lunenburg Middle School provides a rigorous academic curriculum as well as strong programs that support students'
social and emotional growth. These programs ensure that each child becomes a self-motivated, creative, lifelong learner
in a safe, stimulating environment that encourages diversity and open honest communication. The dedicated and
accomplished staff of professionals within the school embraces the philosophy of educating the whole child
academically, socially, and emotionally. This philosophy is a means by which all students become positive community
members that possess the skills to be successful in high school and beyond.
Lunenburg Middle School is in its sixth year as a co-located middle - high school serving grades six through eight.
Effective, student centered middle schools embrace interdisciplinary teams of teachers that enable teachers to work with
smaller groups of students. Smaller groups of students allow teachers to learn and engage students in their preferred
learning style, making them more confident and successful.
Our effective middle school model is student centered and provides opportunities to explore a variety of different
interests and talents through special areas and enrichment classes and extracurricular activities. One of our goals is for
students to discover something they are passionate about and want to continue exploring as they move through high
school and beyond. We will continue to seek out opportunities for students that foster critical thinking and problem
solving skills that prepare them for high school and beyond or where their passion may lead them.
With the return to a sense of normalcy at the beginning of the school year, we are fortunate to not have any mandated
health or safety protocols associated with the global pandemic. We have identified that a large number of students
suffered some type of "learning loss" during the course of the pandemic. This means students may not be functioning at
grade level in the areas of ELA and Math.
In order to combat this learning loss, LMS is utilizing the iReady learning platform to provide an additional learning
component in addition to classroom instruction. iReady is being implemented during our intervention blocks and
provides teachers with individualized learning paths based upon the students individual learning needs. Parents will be
provided fall, winter and spring benchmark assessments created by iReady so they too can monitor student progress.
Lunenburg Middle School has benefited from a top-notch guidance support team that we have had in place since 2021.
Two guidance counselors, a school social worker coupled with our shared school psychologist has been able to provide a
level of social emotional support to our students and their families that we have not been accustomed to. Data supports
the need for these positions as during the pandemic, the number of student's experiencing anxiety and depression has
significantly increased nationwide and in our own community. Our guidance team has been able to meet the needs of our
students while preparing them to be available for academic learning.
Our grade eight team of teachers continue to implement a schedule that mirrors the high school schedule. Our
philosophy is to ease the difficult transition from middle school to the first year of high school by developing student's
independent skills they will require to be successful in high school. Grade eight teachers function as one inclusive team
where students take classes with a variety of different teachers as they would in a high school setting. This differs from
our two interdisciplinary team of teachers that have been a successful model in grades six and seven.

In August of 2022, Lunenburg High School was able to return to school without health and safety protocols due to the
pandemic for the first time in two and a half years. Our entire school community did an outstanding job of educating
students through the pandemic, our efforts now focus on identifying students who were struggling and providing
educational services that would help them succeed in their high school careers and beyond.
One of the components of that support was the addition of a LHS Intervention Teacher. This teaching position was
created in order to provide direct instruction to students who were identified by their teachers as to needing additional
support to be successful in the classroom. Students report to the Interventionist during their study skills block and
receive assistance to the specific class or classes they are struggling in. The initial data collected as to the effectiveness
of this position and the direct impact on students classroom grades and learning are remarkable.
LHS also adopted an additional Algebra Essentials II class that was developed to ensure specific students were able to
access the curriculum and state standards. Creating this additional class benefited all students, as it was able to reduce
class sizes in Algebra II and allow teachers to provide more personalized, individualized instruction while working with
smaller groups of students in a traditionally academically demanding course.
The addition to the faculty and courses at Lunenburg High School have allowed students a more varied options for
course selection, provided individualized and programmatic support and structure for students to be successful. LHS
looks forward to reporting out on the difference in student learning these positions have made.

Given the exciting news that schools could return to 'normal' during the 2021-2022 school year, the Department of
Student Support Services focused its efforts on students' social and emotional wellness. Defining a new normal and
providing structured supports to students as they acclimated to the demands, pace and rigor of academics, vocational
programming and extracurricular activities was a top priority. Staff reflected on student data, strengthened community
partnerships, implemented new initiatives and expanded on the level of tiered supports offered to our student population.
The department continued its important mission to break the stigma of mental health, knowing that everyone adjusts
differently and handles stress in various ways. This unified approach, support, and collaboration helped our student body
display resilience, grow individually, and meet success.
At Monty Tech, we understand that everyone will require help at some point; that as individuals we all have strengths
and weaknesses, and as a result, we strive to implement thoughtful tiered services that promote a feeling of comfort for
students when accessing this support. In addition to the department's current school-based counseling services, Monty
Tech and LUK, Inc. collaborated throughout 2021-2022 with the Department of Public Health to provide services to at-
risk students and their families. The district also partnered with LUK to create a direct pipeline for telehealth referrals
and increased access to counseling supports. Programs such as the HOPE Squad; a peer to peer suicide prevention
program, Project AMP; a program to address prevention of substance use among youth ages 13-17, and Students Taking
A New Direction (STAND); a program to support students displaying at-risk behaviors have all been implemented.
The Department of Student Support Services has taken the necessary measures to ensure Social Emotional Learning
(SEL) is in the forefront of conversations when supporting students as they acclimate to returning to school full time
after lengthy periods of time away. Courses and activities designed to promote mindfulness, understanding, and social
emotional wellness are part of the many course offerings. Yoga and Meditative Art, Visual Arts, Directed Studies with
Social Emotional Learning lessons are all part of the efforts being implemented to ensure we address the needs of all
students and support their individual growth and development in a post pandemic world.

future use and reuse of properties.
